Coinbase's John D'Agostino on why $BTC is holding up

"I'm always very hesitant and concerned about describing any asset, whether it's my old days in commodities or Bitcoin or crypto, as non correlated over the long term. Because as we all know, that correlation tends to hop to one at the worst possible time."

"The answer to why Bitcoin is trading the way it's trading is just a function of its liquidity level. Like lots of other asset classes, it goes through periods of tighter liquidity, and you have these liquidity gaps."

"There's people who postulate that we're gonna have this massive correction in AI and all those hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars of forward investment is gonna shift back into other assets."

"If that is what we had seen over the last few weeks, then we would have seen Bitcoin do more than just tread water."

"I think it's getting some of the runoff. It's also just beneficiary of thinner liquidity than the AI market. The market's not as large as the AI equities market, and so it takes less to hold it up."

"I don't like reading too much into it, but it's nice when we see these handles being held through choppy periods."

Project Eleven co-founder Alex Pruden on why Justin Drake and Yehuda Lindell take different approaches to the quantum threat

"Justin's concern is thinking about the longevity of Ethereum over 50 to 100 years. People who lived through the ETH1 to ETH2 transition remember how painfully long that took and how difficult it was."

"These are decentralized systems. It is very, very difficult to upgrade them. This is not like your phone upgrades and OS kind of thing."

"We need to minimize any kind of possible theoretical risk that might exist in the future. Therefore, we need to do hashes. That's, I think, Justin's perspective. I mean, that's very valid."

"On the flip side, Yehuda, responsible as the chief cryptographer at Coinbase for billions of dollars right now. At this second, his name on the line."

"So can understand why he's maybe got the view that maybe we shouldn't throw away the only thing that we know has worked right now and go into bunker. And I think there's elements of truth to both."

Project Eleven co-founder Conor Deegan: many schemes will fall to quantum and AI in the next five years, and that's a net positive for cryptography

"Yehuda's response is, there is no evidence. These schemes have been around a very long time. And largely, that is true."

"It's quite rare for a cryptographer to go online and say something as direct as a scheme we're all using in production today, that keeps Bitcoin secure, Ethereum secure, the entire Internet secure, banks secure, is going to break without much evidence."

"Whether frontier labs are sitting on a break, the quantum labs are sitting on breaks, obviously, we can't speak to that. We just don't know."

"My take here is schemes will break. We will see lots of schemes fall over the next five years, both to quantum and AI. That's good."

"There's a net positive here for cryptography. We'll always have new schemes to migrate to."

At the start of the conflict, crude rallied because everyone feared the incoming crude shortage (i.e., production shut-in = real loss in barrels).

But as the conflict dragged on, we headed for the proverbial “wall” because of tightness in oil products. Then, in June, they signed the MOU, released 150 million bbls of floating storage, and temporarily resolved the crude issue, while the product issue remained unresolved.

Refining margins skyrocketed, and then everyone thought, “No, no, we have a product shortage.” It’s funny how price action can so easily change a human’s mind.

The 3-2-1 crack spread rallied, and at one point diesel cracks traded higher than crude itself. Great. Refineries made a lot of money, and people thought, “Yeah, we have enough crude, not enough products.”

But then the tanker attacks escalated, and tanker rates started jumping. Then China, after 3 months of not buying crude (exactly the timeframe we thought they could save the world), started buying crude.

Oops, tanker rates started to skyrocket. 

Why? Because now that China wants crude and all those damn tankers want to make the short transit in SOH for 3-4x the pay vs. a long-haul transit, why wouldn’t they?

So they had issues getting tankers to do the other routes, which pushed everything up.
Now those same refineries that benefited from absurd margins are losing money because tanker rates are too high! Oh no, poor refineries.

Asian and European refineries are now contemplating run-cuts because the landed price is negative, which means product tightness will worsen ahead of the winter heating-demand season. Diesel, already super short-supplied, has no room for refinery run-cuts, so prices have to move up again.

But as you can probably tell from what I’m writing so far, none of this is sustainable. Tanker owners, likely seeing this slowdown in demand, will lock in higher rates in other regions, which will cap tanker rates. 

Refineries in Asia and Europe will take advantage of this small dip in tanker rates to lock in whatever crude they can get, which is probably why you are starting to see crude benefit versus both refining margins and tanker rates.

The core of the dilemma from the start is that crude oil has higher storage levels than product storage. That’s not rocket science because crude can be stored for years while petroleum products have an expiration date.

But as you run down all the available crude oil in storage, crude oil will capture any value shift from the other segments. In this case, tanker rates have eaten into what would’ve been the crude value, so this phenomenon will continue over the coming months.

More notably, as we get closer to that operational minimum, crude will rally disproportionately compared with everything else. Again, it’s probably important to say this, but crude has always been the fundamental issue in this conflict.

It's also unnecessarily expensive when liquidity is thin.

Try selling $100K worth of an altcoin through an average orderbook size. Nearly impossible.

→ Request a price for the entire trade
→ Market makers compete with quotes
→ Accept the quote you prefer

All perp trades still execute through Hyperliquid's orderbook. Better prices in the book get priority, while the market maker fills the remainder at the agreed price.

Large trades need this kind of flexibility.
